# Nahum 2 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary

## Overview of the Chapter

Nahum 2 describes the siege, capture, and plundering of Nineveh in extraordinarily vivid poetry. James Montgomery Boice called it “a masterpiece of ancient literature, unsurpassed for its graphic portrayal of a military assault” (enduringword.com). The chapter falls into several movements: a taunting call to battle (vv. 1–2), the chaos of the assault (vv. 3–7), the flight and plunder of the city (vv. 8–10), a sarcastic taunt over the lions’ den (vv. 11–12), and God’s final word of judgment (v. 13).

---

## v. 1 — “One who scatters advances against you, O Nineveh…”

**Traditional Reading:**

The “one who scatters” (or “dasher in pieces” / “the hammer”) is the invading army — the combined forces of the Medes and Babylonians under Cyaxares and Nabopolassar. Gill notes that the Hebrew word can mean “the hammer,” and Babylon itself is called “the hammer of the whole earth” in Jeremiah 50:23. These forces come boldly against Nineveh (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nahum/2.htm).

The four commands — “Guard the fortress! Watch the road! Brace yourselves! Summon all your strength!” — are spoken in biting irony. Ellicott compares them to Elijah’s mocking instructions to the priests of Baal in 1 Kings 18:27. No amount of preparation will save Nineveh. The Pulpit Commentary adds that the loins were regarded as the seat of strength (Job 40:7; 1 Peter 1:13), and that weak, effeminate people were called in Latin *elumbes*, “loinless” (biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/nahum/2.htm).

Constable notes that Nahum used the Hebrew “prophetic perfect” tense — describing future events as though already past — to heighten the certainty of the prophecy. The section has been called “a taunt song” (studylight.org, Constable).

**Denominational Distinctives:**

Baptist commentator Garner-Howes describes verse 1 as the herald announcing that Jehovah Himself “has come upon Nineveh’s face, to confront her in judgment from her evil,” and calls Nineveh “God’s battle-axe” (studylight.org, Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary).

---

## v. 2 — “For the LORD will restore the splendor of Jacob…”

**Traditional Reading:**

This verse is often treated as a parenthetical explanation of *why* Nineveh must fall. The Pulpit Commentary says: “This ruin shall fall on Nineveh because God is mindful of his chosen people, whom Assyria has oppressed” — the Lord “restores the glory and honour of Jacob.” The “emptiers” (the Assyrians) had “emptied them out” and ruined their vine branches, and now payback had come. “Vine branches” is a metaphor for the people of Israel as God’s vineyard (Psalm 80:8; Isaiah 5) (biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/nahum/2.htm).

Ellicott renders it: “For Jehovah restores the glory of Jacob, so that it is as the glory of [ancient] Israel.” He notes that “Jacob” is the birth-name — the nation regarded apart from its religious privileges, the downtrodden exile — while “Israel” is the chosen-of-God name, “he who had power over the angel and prevailed.” The name given by Jehovah is to regain its full significance (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nahum/2.htm).

Gill explains that the Lord “will render a recompense for, or revenge the pride of Jacob” — all the insolence and injuries done by the Assyrian kings. The Assyrians had been God’s rod of chastisement, but now they must suffer for their own excesses (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nahum/2.htm).

Constable notes that the restoration promised probably looks beyond the immediate post-Assyrian period to an ultimate restoration in the Millennium. “Israel” was connected with Israel’s glory while “Jacob” recalls the perverse aspects of national experience (studylight.org, Constable).

**Other Views:**

The Layman’s Bible Commentary notes that the names “Jacob and Israel” are ordinarily designations used for the Northern Kingdom before the fall of Samaria or for Judah after the Exile. The parenthesis “declares the restoration of the people,” with a possible slight change of text yielding the figure of the “grapevine” (studylight.org, Layman's Bible Commentary).

---

## v. 3 — “The shields of his mighty men are red; the valiant warriors are dressed in scarlet…”

**Traditional Reading:**

This verse describes the besieging army in terrifying, colourful detail. “His mighty men” refers to the invaders. The shields are “made red” — either dyed red, or covered in blood, or made of polished copper that glinted red in the sun. Gill notes that red was used partly to inject terror and partly to hide blood so as not to encourage the enemy (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nahum/2.htm).

Ellicott explains that red was the favourite colour of both the Medes and Babylonians (Ezekiel 23:14–15; cf. Xenophon). The phrase translated “flaming torches” in older versions (KJV) is better rendered in the RV as “flash with steel” — referring to steel ornaments or fittings on the chariots that gleamed in the sun. “The cypress [spears] are brandished” — the spears had shafts of fir or cypress wood, just as Homer called the spear “the ash” (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nahum/2.htm).

The Pulpit Commentary discards the “flaming torches” reading, noting that the Hebrew word *peladoth* means “things made of iron or steel.” There is no trace on Assyrian monuments of scythe-chariots, which were unknown before Cyrus. Rather, Assyrian chariots were “conspicuous for shining metal, hung round with gleaming weapons and figures of the heavenly bodies” (biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/nahum/2.htm).

---

## v. 4 — “The chariots dash through the streets; they rush around the plazas…”

**Traditional Reading:**

This continues the picture of the invading chariots raging through the open spaces and broad roads outside the walls. Gill says they “shall be drove in a furious manner from place to place, the men in them breathing out slaughter and death wherever they came.” The comparison to torches and lightning describes their speed and terrifying gleam (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nahum/2.htm).

The Pulpit Commentary explains the besiegers’ chariots appear from the walls so numerous that they seem to “dash against one another,” their gleaming metal making them “appear like torches” — citing 1 Maccabees 6:39, “when the sun shone upon the shields of gold and brass, the mountains glistered therewith, and shined like lamps of fire” (biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/nahum/2.htm).

David Guzik notes that Chuck Smith observed some have “erroneously” taken this as a prophecy of the automobile and traffic congestion (enduringword.com).

Ellicott argues it is “obviously better to restrict the reference throughout to the chariots of the besieged city, darting hither and thither in wild undisciplined attempts to resist the invader’s onset,” rather than seeing it as a description of the Ninevites’ panic (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nahum/2.htm).

---

## v. 5 — “He summons his nobles; they stumble as they advance…”

**Traditional Reading:**

Commentators differ on whether “he” refers to the Assyrian king or the invading commander. Gill offers both views: either the besieging kings call together their officers to encourage them, or the Assyrian king musters his nobles for a counter-attack but “they shall stumble in their walk” — being many and in haste, they stumble and fall upon one another (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nahum/2.htm).

Ellicott sees this as the Assyrian king remembering his stoutest warriors — but “they stumble in their paths in nervous perplexity.” They rush to the wall, only to find the besiegers have already set up their storming-shed (a protective covering for the battering-ram). Ellicott cites Rawlinson’s description of Assyrian siege engines: “All of them were covered with a framework, which was of osier wood, felt, or skins, for the better protection of those who worked the implement” (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nahum/2.htm).

The Pulpit Commentary agrees: “They see the besiegers bringing up their mantelets and towers.” The machine called “the covering” was either a wooden tower or wicker mantelet suspending a battering ram, standing on four or six wheels (biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/nahum/2.htm).

---

## v. 6 — “The river gates are thrown open and the palace collapses.”

**Traditional Reading:**

This is one of the most discussed verses in Nahum. The ancient historian Diodorus Siculus (preserving an account by Ctesias) records that Nineveh’s walls, though immensely thick, were finally breached when “by reason of a continual discharge of great storms, the Euphrates [sic] being swollen, both inundated a part of the city and overthrew the wall to the extent of twenty stadia.” An oracle had declared the city would fall when “the river became an enemy to the city” (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nahum/2.htm).

Ellicott explains that the “gates of the rivers” refer to the dams or sluices that fenced the Khausser (which ran through Nineveh) and the Tigris. When these were forced open by swollen torrents, the walls — built of sun-dried brick or “clay-bat” — were sapped at the foundation. Palace walls were undermined and literally “dissolved.” The verb *nâmôg* (“dissolved”) is taken in its literal sense of dissolution by water (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nahum/2.htm).

Gill also cites the historical tradition: the river Tigris, overflowing, “broke down the walls of the city for two and a half miles, and opened a way for the Medes and Chaldeans to enter.” The “palace” may be the royal palace or the temple of Nisroch, since the same Hebrew word can mean either (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nahum/2.htm).

Gaebelein notes the parallel with Babylon’s fall: “when Babylon fell, under the grandson of Nebuchadnezzar, the river also was the means of defeat, for the enemy had diverted the river Euphrates and through the dry river-bed entered the city” (studylight.org, Gaebelein).

---

## v. 7 — “It is decreed that the city be exiled and carried away…”

**Traditional Reading:**

The BSB’s “It is decreed” represents a famous translation crux. The KJV reads “And Huzzab shall be led away captive,” treating *Huzzab* as a proper name — either a queen or a symbolic name for Nineveh. The Pulpit Commentary explains this as an appellative meaning “established” or “firm,” from the root *natsab*, “to set” or “to fix” — thus “the firmly established one” is led captive (biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/nahum/2.htm).

Ellicott and many modern commentators prefer “And it is decided. She is laid bare. She is removed away.” The word *hutstsab* is taken as a verb form cognate to expressions meaning “certain” or “true” in Daniel. Ellicott: “c’est un fait accompli.” The “maidens” who “moan as with the cry of doves” are probably Nineveh’s dependent cities, standing gazing on the catastrophe, groaning and beating the breast in horror (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nahum/2.htm).

Gill notes the Targum translates it “the queen,” and some rabbinic commentators (Jarchi, Aben Ezra) take it as the name of the queen of Assyria. He also notes that some historians describe the last Assyrian king as effeminate — “conversing only with women; imitating their voice; wearing their apparel; and doing their work, spinning” (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nahum/2.htm).

Gaebelein agrees: “We believe the word ‘Huzzab’ should be translated, ‘it is determined.’ Then the sentence reads, ‘It is determined; she is made bare and led away captive; and her maids moan like the doves, smiting upon their breasts’” (studylight.org, Gaebelein).

---

## v. 8 — “Nineveh has been like a pool of water throughout her days…”

**Traditional Reading:**

The Pulpit Commentary explains: Nineveh is compared to a pool or reservoir from the multitude of her inhabitants gathered from all parts of the world, both as tributaries and for commerce (cf. Jeremiah 51:13; Revelation 17:1, 15). “Yet they shall flee away” — the multitudes represented by “the waters” fly before the enemy. In vain the captains cry “Stand, stand!” — no one turns back (biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/nahum/2.htm).

Gill says the city was “like a fish pool, full of people,” as in the days of Jonah, “full of wealth and riches,” and “like a pool of standing water, had never been liable to any commotions and disturbances, but had remained from the beginning in a tranquil and prosperous state.” Now the waters drain out as the sluices are opened — the people flee. The cry “Stand, stand!” may be from the Assyrian officers, from courageous inhabitants, or even from the enemy promising to spare those who surrender (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nahum/2.htm).

Ellicott prefers a textual emendation following the LXX: “And Nineveh, like a pool of water are her waters, and they [her inhabitants] are fleeing away” — the waters that formerly flowed in orderly river-courses and dykes are now one vast expanse of inundation (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nahum/2.htm).

Guzik summarizes: “Nahum said the troops defending Nineveh would be like a pool of water that drains away to no use. They would be useless in defending the city” (enduringword.com).

---

## v. 9 — “Plunder the silver! Plunder the gold! There is no end to the treasure…”

**Traditional Reading:**

The invaders are called — by the prophet or by God — to seize the spoil. Gill relates the ancient accounts: the Assyrian king, seeing all was lost, built a funeral pile, heaped his gold, silver, and royal apparel upon it, and burned himself with his eunuchs and concubines. Athenaeus claimed there were “no less in this pile than a thousand myriads of talents of gold, which are about fourteen hundred millions sterling, and ten times as many talents of silver” — yet after all this, the Babylonians and Medes still carried off vast quantities (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nahum/2.htm).

The Pulpit Commentary cites similar accounts: “Sardanapalus is said to have placed a hundred and fifty golden beds, and as many tables of the same metal, on his funeral pile, besides gold and silver vases and ornaments in enormous quantities.” Bonomi notes that neither Botta nor Layard found any of that store of silver and gold — “scarcely anything, even of bronze, escaped the spoiler” (biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/nahum/2.htm).

Guzik quotes Boice: “An impressive confirmation of this prophecy is that nothing of all this gold and silver has been discovered in the ruins of Nineveh by archaeologists. Nineveh was indeed stripped bare” (enduringword.com).

---

## v. 10 — “She is emptied! Yes, she is desolate and laid waste!…”

**Traditional Reading:**

The Hebrew uses three very similar-sounding words for devastating effect: *bukah umebukah umebullakah*. The Pulpit Commentary calls it a “paronomasia” — an alliterative word-play — and offers various attempts to capture it: “vacuitas, evacuatio, evanidatio” (Latin); “Sack and sacking and ransacking” (Gandell); “leer und ausgeleert und verheert” (German) (biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/nahum/2.htm).

Constable notes that the Hebrew words “sound like water flowing out of a bottle when read aloud, a literary device called onomatopoeia. Even the sound of the description of Nineveh’s fall reinforced the prophecy” (studylight.org, Constable).

The rest of the verse piles up physical symptoms of terror: melting hearts (Joshua 7:5; Isaiah 13:7), knocking knees (Daniel 5:6), anguish like childbirth in the loins, and faces that “gather blackness” — a livid, deathly pallor. The LXX renders it “as the burning of an earthen vessel, which is blackened by the fire” (biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/nahum/2.htm).

Gill adds that the Targum compares the faces to “a pot” — being in great distress and disconsolation, making men’s countenances look dark and gloomy (Joel 2:6) (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nahum/2.htm).

---

## v. 11 — “Where is the lions’ lair…?”

**Traditional Reading:**

The lion was the national emblem of Assyria. It appears “so frequently on the Assyrian monuments that we may perhaps suppose it to have been a national scutcheon” (Ellicott). Nergal, the Assyrian war god, had a winged lion with a man’s face as his emblem (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nahum/2.htm and biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/nahum/2.htm).

The question “Where is the dwelling of the lions?” is a taunt — “What has happened to the lions’ den?” The obvious answer: the lion will no longer bring prey for the lionesses and cubs. The conquests of Nineveh are at an end. The Pulpit Commentary explains the various terms — the full-grown male lion, the lioness, the young lion able to seek its own food, and the whelp — may refer to different ranks of satraps and chieftains in the Assyrian kingdom. “They lived in perfect security, without fear or care, irresistible in might” (biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/nahum/2.htm).

Gill likens the kings of Assyria — Pul, Tiglath-pileser, Shalmaneser, Sennacherib — to lions for “their strength, courage, and cruelty, tyranny, and oppression.” The Targum paraphrases: “Where are the habitations of kings?” (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nahum/2.htm).

Guzik adds: Nahum asked “Where is the dwelling of the lions?” because “God would bring them low, who once were so mighty” (enduringword.com).

---

## v. 12 — “The lion mauled enough for its cubs…”

**Traditional Reading:**

The metaphor continues in loose apposition to verse 11: where is the lion that used to tear in pieces enough for its whelps? The Assyrian monarch provided for his children and dependents by plundering other nations. “His lionesses” may mean his wives and concubines. The Pulpit Commentary notes: “It was the custom both with the Persians and Assyrians to assign towns and provinces to their favourites. Xenophon mentions certain villages as set apart for the girdle of Queen Parysatis” — and Cicero mentions the same practice (biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/nahum/2.htm).

Gill: “Thus the Assyrians made war on other nations, and pillaged and plundered them, to enlarge their dominions, provide for their posterity, and enrich their children.” He notes the Targum: “kings bring rapine to their wives, and a prey to their children” (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nahum/2.htm).

The Bridgeway Bible Commentary summarizes: “So ruthless and cruel were the Assyrians in their treatment of the nations they attacked, that the prophet likens them to wild animals. They are like ferocious lions that savagely attacked smaller helpless animals and then dragged them back to their den. But now the lions are dead and the den is empty” (studylight.org, Bridgeway).

---

## v. 13 — “Behold, I am against you, declares the LORD of Hosts…”

**Traditional Reading:**

This is the climactic word of judgment. God Himself speaks directly. Gill writes: “If he, who is the Lord of hosts, of all the armies of heaven and earth, was against them, nothing but ruin must inevitably ensue.” The title “LORD of hosts” refers to God as commander-in-chief over all the armies of heaven. The Targum renders it: “Behold, I will send my fury upon thee” (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nahum/2.htm).

Guzik draws out the theological force: “What a terrible thing to hear from God! The principle of Romans 8:31 is true for the believer: If God is for us, who can be against us? Accordingly, the opposite is also true — if God is against you, then who can be for you?” (enduringword.com).

Each element of the judgment is specific:
- **“I will send your chariots up in smoke”** — Gill says this means they will burn “easily, quickly, at once, suddenly, so that they should evaporate into smoke, and be no more” or “with a great fire, whose smoke is seen afar off” (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nahum/2.htm).
- **“The sword will devour your young lions”** — the young warriors or princes of Assyria will be cut down.
- **“I will cut off your prey from the earth”** — no more plundering of other nations.
- **“The voices of your messengers will no longer be heard”** — Nineveh’s heralds and delegates, who once carried threats and demands for tribute to subject kingdoms, would fall silent forever. Ellicott notes these were “royal heralds and delegates, subordinate agents in this business of extortion” (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nahum/2.htm).

Constable adds: “If Nineveh could fall, would anything be secure?” — the terror was meant to be universal (studylight.org, Constable).

The Layman’s Bible Commentary concludes that the poet-prophet was right. Though a new king, Ashuruballit, attempted to establish continuing Assyrian rule at Harran after the fall of Nineveh, his efforts were doomed. “The remnants of Assyrian power were gathered up by the Babylonians within a few years” (studylight.org, Layman's Bible Commentary).

---

## Points of Denominational Emphasis

**Reformed / Ligonier:** While no specific Ligonier page on Nahum 2 was retrievable, the Desiring God article on Nahum (Baptist/Reformed in orientation) stresses the theological meaning of God’s wrath displayed in nature and history: “Strong storms that flash and rage… symbolize the frightening words uttered by God against unrepentant sinners: ‘Behold, I am against you’ (Nahum 2:13; 3:5).” The article emphasises that Nahum’s prophecy was “no hyperbolic description” — every word came to pass — and that God’s “slowness to anger” (which Nineveh experienced in Jonah’s day) does not mean He will not finally judge (desiringgod.org).

**Baptist:** The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary emphasises God’s direct agency: it is Jehovah who “has come upon Nineveh’s face” as the one who “dasheth” — Nineveh is called “God’s battle-axe” (studylight.org). The Bridgeway Commentary (broadly evangelical/Baptist context) highlights the moral dimension: Nineveh was “destroyed because of cruelty.”

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / Chuck Smith):** David Guzik, drawing from the Calvary Chapel tradition, notes Chuck Smith’s comment that some have mistakenly seen modern automobiles and traffic in the description of chariots racing like torches and lightning. This reflects the Pentecostal/Charismatic interest in seeing possible end-times imagery in prophetic texts, though Guzik labels it “erroneous” (enduringword.com).

---

## Other Views

**Modern Scholarship (NET Bible notes):** No specific NET Bible notes page was retrieved for Nahum 2. However, Constable’s notes (which engage with modern scholarship) note the chiastic structure of the passage, the use of the Hebrew prophetic perfect, and the onomatopoeia in verse 10. He also notes the millennial interpretation — that the restoration promised in verse 2 “will take place in the Millennium” (studylight.org, Constable).

**Catholic and Orthodox:** No direct Catholic or Orthodox commentary pages on Nahum 2 were found in the search results. The Pulpit Commentary occasionally references the Vulgate and Septuagint readings, and Gill references the Apocrypha (Tobit 14:15) regarding the historical fall of Nineveh — that Nabopolassar and Cyaxares together took the city. These sources do not however represent a distinctively Catholic or Orthodox *theological* reading.

**Debated Popular Teaching:** Guzik notes (refuting it) that some have interpreted the chariots “running like lightning” in verse 4 as a prophecy of modern automobiles — this is associated with some popular end-times speculation, but no mainstream commentary endorses it (enduringword.com).
